---
title: "Poisson maximum likelihood"
execute:
  enabled: true

The Bernoulli likelihood represented one case label per token. A different question asks how many annotated personal pronouns occur in one BOUN sentence. The response is now a nonnegative count, including sentences with no qualifying pronoun.

The [Poisson distribution](../random-variables-and-distributions/poisson-distribution.qmd#definition-and-fit) is a useful first count model when sentences have a common exposure and pronoun-occurrence opportunities can be treated as approximately independent with a stable rate. Those assumptions are provisional here: sentences differ in length and construction, and sentence counts may share document and register contexts. A defining implication is $\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=\operatorname{Var}[Y_i]=\lambda$, which gives us a direct adequacy check.

We first construct one count per BOUN sentence, then derive the Poisson maximum-likelihood estimator, and finally compare the fitted mean with the empirical variance before deciding how much the working model can support.

## Constructing the sentence counts

The full UD Turkish BOUN 2.18 release defines the sentence total used below. The pronoun extract identifies every sentence with at least one selected token; subtracting those distinct identifiers from the release total reconstructs the zero count exactly. The zero rows lack recoverable document or register identifiers, so the analysis cannot model those sources of structure.

```{r}
#| label: build-ud-sentence-counts
library(ggplot2)

pronouns <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/personal-pronoun-cases.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
release_sentence_total <- 9761L
positive_counts <- as.integer(table(pronouns$sentence_id))
zero_count <- release_sentence_total - length(positive_counts)
sentence_counts <- c(positive_counts, rep.int(0L, zero_count))

stopifnot(
  length(sentence_counts) == release_sentence_total,
  sum(sentence_counts) == nrow(pronouns),
  zero_count == 8034L
)
```

## Deriving the Poisson estimator

Suppose, as a working model, that

$$
Y_i\mathrel{\overset{\mathrm{IID}}{\sim}}\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda).
$$

For one sentence,

$$
p(y_i\mid\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^{y_i}e^{-\lambda}}{y_i!}.
$$

The support includes zero. Indeed, a zero-pronoun sentence contributes $e^{-\lambda}$ to the likelihood. Removing such sentences would condition on $Y_i>0$ and change both the model and the estimand.

The likelihood and log likelihood are

$$
L(\lambda;\mathbf y)
=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\lambda^{y_i}e^{-\lambda}}{y_i!}
$$

and

$$
\ell(\lambda)
=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\right)\log\lambda
-n\lambda
-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(y_i!).
$$

The final term depends on the observed counts but not on $\lambda$. It can be dropped when locating the maximizing $\lambda$, though it remains part of the normalized probability model.

Thus

$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\lambda}
=\frac{\sum_i y_i}{\lambda}-n,
$$

and setting the score to zero gives

$$
\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{MLE}}
=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i
=\overline y.
$$

## Fit and model check

```{r}
#| label: fit-ud-sentence-poisson
lambda_hat <- mean(sentence_counts)
empirical_variance <- mean((sentence_counts - lambda_hat)^2)
variance_to_mean <- empirical_variance / lambda_hat

count_grid <- data.frame(count = 0:max(sentence_counts))
observed_table <- table(factor(sentence_counts, levels = count_grid$count))
count_grid$observed_probability <- as.numeric(observed_table) / length(sentence_counts)
count_grid$fitted_probability <- dpois(count_grid$count, lambda_hat)

observed_zero <- mean(sentence_counts == 0) # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
fitted_zero <- dpois(0, lambda_hat)
observed_two_or_more <- mean(sentence_counts >= 2) # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
fitted_two_or_more <- ppois(1, lambda_hat, lower.tail = FALSE)

stopifnot(abs(lambda_hat - nrow(pronouns) / release_sentence_total) < 1e-12)

data.frame(
  lambda_mle = lambda_hat,
  empirical_variance = empirical_variance,
  variance_to_mean = variance_to_mean,
  observed_zero = observed_zero,
  fitted_zero = fitted_zero,
  observed_two_or_more = observed_two_or_more,
  fitted_two_or_more = fitted_two_or_more
)
```

The fitted mean is `r sprintf("%.4f", lambda_hat)` pronouns per sentence. But the empirical variance is `r sprintf("%.4f", empirical_variance)`, producing a variance-to-mean ratio of `r sprintf("%.3f", variance_to_mean)` rather than the Poisson value of one.

```{r}
#| label: plot-ud-sentence-poisson
#| fig-cap: "Observed sentence-count probabilities and probabilities under the fitted Poisson model."
ggplot(count_grid, aes(count)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed_probability), color = "grey25", size = 2.1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted_probability), color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(y = fitted_probability), color = "#8B1A1A", size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = count_grid$count) +
  labs(x = "Annotated personal pronouns per sentence", y = "Proportion of BOUN sentences") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The observed zero proportion is `r sprintf("%.4f", observed_zero)`, compared with `r sprintf("%.4f", fitted_zero)` under the fitted model. The mismatch shows that maximizing a likelihood does not guarantee adequate fit. It does not, by itself, identify register, document, or syntactic structure as the source of extra variation.

The formula-to-code bridge is short: `mean(sentence_counts)` evaluates $\overline y=\widehat\lambda$, `dpois()` evaluates fitted point probabilities, and the empirical variance-to-mean ratio checks the Poisson equality of mean and variance.

## Recap and forward link

1. The Poisson is a working model for nonnegative counts with a common rate and equal mean and variance.
2. Zero-count sentences belong to the target sentence population and affect the likelihood.
3. The log-factorial term can be omitted for maximization only because it is constant in $\lambda$.
4. A maximum-likelihood fit can still miss the observed count distribution.

The [independence-testing pages](fishers-exact-test.qmd#the-conditional-probability) next move from sentence counts to contingency tables.

## Check your understanding

1. Why must zero-pronoun sentences enter the likelihood?
2. Show how the Poisson score equation yields the sample mean.
3. Which visible feature of the fitted distribution misses the data?
4. Why can we not diagnose document clustering from this prepared count vector?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Zero-count sentences are part of the sentence population and contribute the factor $e^{-\lambda}$; excluding them would condition on observing at least one pronoun and inflate the fitted mean. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Setting $\partial\ell/\partial\lambda=(\sum_i y_i)/\lambda-n$ to zero gives $\widehat\lambda=(\sum_i y_i)/n=\overline y$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The fitted Poisson probabilities miss the observed count shape, including the observed mass at zero and the heavier occurrence of multiple-pronoun sentences. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The reconstructed zero rows have no document identifiers, so the prepared vector cannot show which sentences share documents. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](properties-of-estimators.qmd) treats an estimator as a random variable across repeated samples.
